en: Seitek, who saw the turn,
Mourning his father,
Crying and screaming
Disappointed,
Tears in his eyes.
Every brother left by my father,
When the animal is standing like this
I was the son's offspring,
It's really summer
I wish I could see it with my own eyes.
Twisting around
The horse is watching,
Separate tears,
It pours from every steam.
When Buurul stood like this,
Seitek, son of the hero
Disappointed, separated
Tears in his eyes,
The right rib
Separated from letter to letter,
A horse from an animal
How does father Semetei look like?
Like a fly, the soul is chirping,
The bones are broken,
Buurul horse,
What does the father look like
Tears poured into his bosom,
It happened to Buurul,
My property left by my father,
This is not my money
My soul is hot in the sky.
Buurul came to meet,
My blood has broken today.
My soul burned with fire,
I am an orphan, wandering cattle,
Shame on you.
Twelve signed,
I'm sorry, my father
Talas is a vast land
A pillar of gold,
When the name is like this
I lost my father
This soul is so vulnerable,
Detached from the statue.
Sold to a caravan,
They were hidden together.
Without a beak from an animal,
Where are you salty?
Father did not smell,
Just look at the arcade
He sniffed him deeply, again and again,
From my father who passed before,
He sniffed him, saying, “You remain as my inheritance,”
And while Seytek stood weeping,
Aichürök came wailing bitterly.
When she saw the dapple-gray steed,
Your ill-fated noble sister-in-law
Clawed her face and shrieked:
“His horse remains, but he is gone,
My noble-hearted lord is nowhere to be seen,
Is this what you are, filthy world?”
So Aichürök lamented,
“My precious one’s noble steed,
Would not tire when ridden on patrol,
Would not weary after six months’ riding,
Until he reached sixty years of age
His fangs would not jut out, nor would he grow old,
He would not falter when ridden into combat.
He would not sicken when ridden with the baggage train;
But you are here, and the hero is gone.
When I think of it, what dreadful misery!
My ruined lord, come and take him!”
So Aichürök
Raised her voice in a piercing cry,
And at her white face, fair as a plane tree,
She tore and tore;
Dark blood flowed where she clawed,
And all strength left your sister-in-law.
Her gray pacer went ambling on,
While the blood streaming down both cheeks
Flowed over the gray pacer’s mane,
Running down a whip-length.
Overcome by grievous affliction,
She threw herself down when she saw him.
Shrieking at the sight of Buurul,
Poor Aichürök
Fell down as though dead.
She had settled at the cliffside camp,
Bereft of her noble-hearted lord,
And had come to bear a wretched name.
Before my lion-hearted father,
If only I might die as a sacrifice!
When even a beast grieves like this,
I am human—I am his son;
How can I endure it,
When the beast comes neighing,
Lamenting thunderously beneath me?
The beast spoke a word
That said, “Let my noble father not be dead.”
It drove a thought into my breast:
“If my lion-hearted father were alive,
Leading the way and fighting foes,
If my bloodthirsty father were here,
I would don my chain-mail cap
And strike the enemy head-on.
With my noble, lion-hearted father,
I did not die as his companion;
I did not crush the approaching enemy,
Nor tear them limb from limb.
My precious heroic father’s
Robe worn on ceremonial occasions—
I did not put on that bulletproof coat.
If my dear father were alive,
I would ask for and mount my Buurul,
The steed no bullet could reach,
And charge the foe with a battle cry.
With my lion-hearted father,
I never rode as his companion.
I am left an ill-fated orphan;
My leopard of a father, come and take me.
Your beast stands neighing,
Your orphan stands crying aloud.
My father is gone—what cruel fate!
My devastated father, to whom all twelve
Pledged their united allegiance, come and take me!
Saying, “My sole beast left from the host,”
And, “Though a beast, he is my very soul,”
He pressed his face to the horse’s chest,
Grasped its forelock and sniffed it sorrowfully,
And clasped the noble steed in his arms.
Unable to take his tiny life,
His grief and humiliation
The bloodthirsty warrior’s son, brave Seytek,
Could not master with courage;
“Restrain your grief.
Before the spoken words could be gathered,
Before anyone could say, ‘What is it?’
In the blink of an eye,
Sixty mighty caravan men,
Those fiends who stole horses,
Their shouts loud enough to split stone,
Their cries loud enough to shatter heads,
Roared, “Where is the enemy?”
And challenged, “Come out in single combat!”
Gripping battle-axes, they made ready;
Whichever one you looked at
Swayed as if eager to grapple.
They brandished unsheathed swords
And merely gnashed apart
Their shovel-like teeth.
They bounded like tigers,
As though none who fought them could survive.
The sixty mighty caravan men
Brandished their lances,
And swung their crescent-bladed axes.
They thrust forward their cast-iron mace heads,
Swaggering and working themselves into a fury.
Toward Seytek, who stood grieving,
They came calling him a bandit;
The strongmen were approaching
As though to lash and beat him,
Their words vile, their faces grim,
As though they would destroy him utterly.
Those hulking brutes,
Those boundlessly insolent thugs,
If left to their own devices,
Looked ready to mow down and seize everything.
The lumbering caravan men
Had hell showing in their faces,
Intent on stirring every kind of quarrel.
My tunic, blue-mottled as a lake,
She had torn open and cast aside;
When she saw noble Buurul,
Your precious mother Aichürök
Had fallen down as though dead.
Aichürök stood shrieking,
Seytek sobbed and wept,
The speechless horse Buurul wept,
Everyone who beheld them wept,
The people watching wept,
The broad-breasted earth itself wept.
His face went pale and wan,
And the tears flowing from both eyes
Poured down over his chest.
They gathered all along the cliffside camp,
As if the colossal, mountain-like lion
Had only just died.
Their bellies churned and their souls burned,
Their bodies went limp and their blood burned;
The world closed in around them,
And anguish smoldered within.
As though the bloodthirsty gray-maned hero had died,
As though they had seen calamity that very day,
They sobbed and wept, yet could not die,
Unable to take their own lives.
Snot streamed from their noses like spring water,
And they rode on, weeping convulsively,
Standing there bereft of strength,
Their thoughts utterly distracted.
The gray-maned hero’s Buurul
Appeared before his eyes exactly like
His lion-hearted father Semetey.
Every joint trembled and gave way,
And the orphan wailed in anguish.
To the lion-hearted son of his father,
His father’s heavenly steed,
Noble Buurul, appeared before him,
And when the orphan saw him,
Tears poured from his eyes.
He wished to die, yet could not die.
Have I taken your piebald horse?
Have I chased away your wild ass?
You swaggering caravan men,
Have I scattered the money from your saddlebags?
You began this wrongdoing yourselves,
You blustering caravan men;
Now see what sport you will get from me!
You say, “Give us your bundled money,”
And, “Obey what we say at once.”
Which of you have I wronged?
I have committed no offense today;
You sixty mighty caravan men,
Why have you provoked my anger?
When did I ever enrage you
By demanding half your money?
My wrath is rising; I stand unyielding,
I will not spare a single one of you.
Why did you rouse my fury?
You have sorely offended my spirit;
I let it pass unnoticed, caravan men.
You are turning this into an ugly quarrel;
If I simply leave you to yourselves,
You strike people with cast-iron maces.
All sixty of you band together,
Halting wherever you please,
And cursing mothers and daughters.
You have gone rabid, you unruly caravan men,
Swaggering in your insolence.
Refusing to leave peaceful people alone,
Why have you provoked my anger?
My wrath is rising; I stand unyielding;
Now I will not leave
A single one of you untouched!
I will plunder your livestock,
Cut short every one of your lives,
And, as though a terrible slaughter had struck,
Destroy you all!
You blustering caravan men,
Your guilt is upon your own heads,
And your punishment upon your black crowns!”
His courage was as hard as his loins.
To hear his battle cry,
It was like an icy gorge wind.
If left alone, he would finish them utterly,
And reclaim
The aged Buurul.
